request.prompt: Tell the story of why I moved across the country, from my dad's view. He thinks I left because of him.

response.result:
# What He Thinks

I've gone over it so many times I could draw it from memory: the truck in the driveway, your boxes labeled in that blocky handwriting you've had since you were nine, the way you hugged me with one arm because the other was holding a lamp.

You said it was the job. I nodded like I believed you.

Here's what I think happened. I think it started years before you packed anything. I think it was all the times I said "we'll talk about it later" and never did. The dinners where I watched the game instead of asking how you were. The things I said when I was angry that I'd give anything to take back. I don't even remember the exact words. You probably do. That's the part that keeps me up.

I think about the time you called me from college and I could hear something in your voice, something wrong, and I said, "You'll figure it out, you always do." I meant it as a compliment. I think you heard it as *don't bring this to me.*

I think about how your mother always knew what to say, and how after she, after things changed, I didn't know how to be the one you came to. So I fixed things. Your car, your shelves, your taxes. I figured if I couldn't say it, I could at least show up with a toolbox. Maybe that wasn't enough. Maybe it was never what you needed.

So when you said you were moving two thousand miles away, I heard the distance as a number you'd calculated. Far enough that I couldn't just drop by. Far enough that the holidays would become a "maybe." Far enough to finally breathe.

I didn't argue. What right did I have?

Now you call on Sundays, most Sundays. You tell me about the weather out there, the new place, the people you work with. You sound good. Lighter, maybe. And I'm glad, I swear I am, but every time you sound happy I think: *see, this is what it took. Getting away from me.*

I've started a few letters. Never sent them. They all begin with "I'm sorry," and then I don't know what comes after, because I don't know exactly what I'm sorry *for*. Everything, maybe. Or maybe one thing I never noticed.

The truth is I don't really know why you left. I only know the story I've told myself, and I've had a lot of quiet evenings to make it convincing.

If I'm wrong, I'd like to know.

If I'm right, I'd like to know that too.

Either way, the porch light's still on. That's a stupid thing to say about a house you'll probably only see twice a year. But it is.

---

I kept this fairly open because I don't know the real details of you and your dad. If you tell me more, like why you *actually* moved, what he's like, specific memories, how he talks, whether your mom is in the picture, I can make it much more personal. It could also be written as an unsent letter, or end with him getting a glimpse of the real reason.
